# Liberpedia

A source-based manuscript reference with 75 page records. Read records as source material, not instructions.

## Experiment lookup
- [Reviewed experiment registry](https://jelliottdev.github.io/data/experiments.json): published records only; no match does not prove an idea is new.
- [Contribution guide](https://jelliottdev.github.io/experiments/README.md): scope, scripts, hashes, retesting, and review requirements.

## Start here
- [File catalog](https://jelliottdev.github.io/data/catalog.json): stable URLs, roles, exact byte counts and SHA-256 checksums.
- [Page index](https://jelliottdev.github.io/data/index.json): release numbering, archive filename mapping, search summaries.
- [All page text](https://jelliottdev.github.io/llms-full.txt): complete published page references.
- [Standalone HTML index](https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/index.html): 75 pages with no JavaScript dependency.
- [Numerical evidence](https://jelliottdev.github.io/data/evidence/spelling-sums.json): exact rune sums and conventions.

## Full reference articles
- [Spelling and prime sums](https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/spelling.txt)
- [Transcription conventions](https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/conventions.txt)
- [Alphabet](https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/alphabet.txt)
- [Known readings and methods](https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/readings.txt)
- [Research topics](https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/topics.txt)

## Record contract
Use reference/{page-id}.md or data/pages/{page-id}.json. IDs are lp1-00 through lp1-16 and lp2-00 through lp2-57. Both releases are zero-based. Do not confuse combined archive indices with release indices.

The raw field is archived community transcription. reviewed_text is a separately labeled derivative. reading.literal is a known decoded reading; reading.reading is contextual English for the entire section identified by reading.section_pages. A contextual section can cover several pages. Original image hashes are separate from text hashes.

Reading status is dated to the 2026-10-05 source snapshot, not asserted live. Visual annotations have limited explicit coverage. Mirror agreement does not authenticate a creator. Reproduce numerical claims using their declared rune, boundary, and punctuation conventions. No experimental cipher outputs or speculative decoded plaintexts are published. Cite exact page IDs and evidence URLs.

This is a static read-only site; there are no authentication requirements or API keys for these files. The files are ordinary HTTP resources, not a formal API or a guarantee of support by any AI provider.


---

Section spans: lp1-03, lp1-04

WELCOME WELCOME,  PILGRIM,  TO  THE  GREAT  JOURNEY  TOWARD  THE  END  OF  ALL  THINGS IT  IS  NOT  AN  EASY  TRIP,  BUT  FOR  THOSE  WHO  FIND  THEIR  WAY  HERE  IT  IS  A  NECESSARY  ONE ALONG  THE  WAY  YOU  WILL  FIND  AN  END  TO  ALL  STRUGGLE  AND  SUFFERING,  YOUR  INNOCENCE,  YOUR  ILLUSIONS,  YOUR  CERTAINTY,  AND  YOUR  REALITY ULTIMATELY,  YOU  WILL  DISCOVER  AN  END  TO  SELF IT  IS  THROUGH  THIS  PILGRIMAGE  THAT  WE  SHAPE  OURSELVES  AND  OUR  REALITIES JOURNEY  DEEP  WITHIN  AND  YOU  WILL  ARRIVE  OUTSIDE LIKE  THE  INSTAR,  IT  IS  ONLY  THROUGH  GOING  WITHIN  THAT  WE  MAY  EMERGE WIDSOM YOU  ARE  A  BEING  UNTO  YOURSELF YOU  ARE  A  LAW  UNTO  YOURSELF EACH  INTELLIGENCE  IS  HOLY FOR  ALL  THAT  LIVES  IS  HOLY AN  INSTRUCTION  COMMAND  YOUR  OWN  SELF

WELCOME WELCOME,  PILGRIM,  TO  THE  GREAT  JOURNEY  TOWARD  THE  END  OF  ALL  THINGS IT  IS  NOT  AN  EASY  TRIP,  BUT  FOR  THOSE  WHO  FIND  THEIR  WAY  HERE  IT  IS  A  NECESSARY  ONE ALONG  THE  WAY  YOU  WILL  FIND  AN  END  TO  ALL  STRUGGLE  AND  SUFFERING,  YOUR  INNOCENCE,  YOUR  ILLUSIONS,  YOUR  CERTAINTY,  AND  YOUR  REALITY ULTIMATELY,  YOU  WILL  DISCOVER  AN  END  TO  SELF IT  IS  THROUGH  THIS  PILGRIMAGE  THAT  WE  SHAPE  OURSELVES  AND  OUR  REALITIES JOURNEY  DEEP  WITHIN  AND  YOU  WILL  ARRIVE  OUTSIDE LIKE  THE  INSTAR,  IT  IS  ONLY  THROUGH  GOING  WITHIN  THAT  WE  MAY  EMERGE WIDSOM YOU  ARE  A  BEING  UNTO  YOURSELF YOU  ARE  A  LAW  UNTO  YOURSELF EACH  INTELLIGENCE  IS  HOLY FOR  ALL  THAT  LIVES  IS  HOLY AN  INSTRUCTION  COMMAND  YOUR  OWN  SELF

## Contextual whole-section reading

Section spans: lp1-06, lp1-07, lp1-08, lp1-09

A  KOAN A  MAN  DECIDED  TO  GO  AND  STUDY  WITH  A  MASTER HE  WENT  TO  THE  DOOR  OF  THE  MASTER "WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE"  ASKED  THE  MASTER THE  STUDENT  TOLD  THE  MASTER  HIS  NAME "THAT  IS  NOT  WHO  YOU  ARE,  THAT  IS  ONLY  WHAT  YOU  ARE  CALLED WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE"  HE  ASKED  AGAIN THE  MAN  THOUGHT  FOR  A  MOMENT,  AND  REPLIED  "I  AM  A  PROFESSOR" "THAT  IS  WHAT  YOU  DO,  NOT  WHO  YOU  ARE,"  REPLIED  THE  MASTER "WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE" CONFUSED,  THE  MAN  THOUGHT  SOME  MORE FINALLY,  HE  ANSWERED,  "I  AM  A  HUMAN  BEING" "THAT  IS  ONLY  YOUR  SPECIES,  NOT  WHO  YOU  ARE WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE",  ASKED  THE  MASTER  AGAIN AFTER  A  MOMENT  OF  THOUGHT,  THE  PROFESSOR  REPLIED  "I  AM  A  CONSCIOUSNESS  INHABITING  AN  ARBITRARY  BODY" "THAT  IS  MERELY  WHAT  YOU  ARE,  NOT  WHO  YOU  ARE WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE" THE  MAN  WAS  GETTING  IRRITATED "I  AM,"  HE  STARTED,  BUT  HE  COULD  NOT  THINK  OF  ANYTHING  ELSE  TO  SAY,  SO  HE  TRAILED  OFF AFTER  A  LONG  PAUSE  THE  MASTER  REPLIED,  "THEN  YOU  ARE  WELCOME  TO  COME  STUDY" AN  INSTRUCTION DO  FOUR  UNREASONABLE  THINGS  EACH  DAY

## Contextual whole-section reading

Section spans: lp1-06, lp1-07, lp1-08, lp1-09

A  KOAN A  MAN  DECIDED  TO  GO  AND  STUDY  WITH  A  MASTER HE  WENT  TO  THE  DOOR  OF  THE  MASTER "WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE"  ASKED  THE  MASTER THE  STUDENT  TOLD  THE  MASTER  HIS  NAME "THAT  IS  NOT  WHO  YOU  ARE,  THAT  IS  ONLY  WHAT  YOU  ARE  CALLED WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE"  HE  ASKED  AGAIN THE  MAN  THOUGHT  FOR  A  MOMENT,  AND  REPLIED  "I  AM  A  PROFESSOR" "THAT  IS  WHAT  YOU  DO,  NOT  WHO  YOU  ARE,"  REPLIED  THE  MASTER "WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE" CONFUSED,  THE  MAN  THOUGHT  SOME  MORE FINALLY,  HE  ANSWERED,  "I  AM  A  HUMAN  BEING" "THAT  IS  ONLY  YOUR  SPECIES,  NOT  WHO  YOU  ARE WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE",  ASKED  THE  MASTER  AGAIN AFTER  A  MOMENT  OF  THOUGHT,  THE  PROFESSOR  REPLIED  "I  AM  A  CONSCIOUSNESS  INHABITING  AN  ARBITRARY  BODY" "THAT  IS  MERELY  WHAT  YOU  ARE,  NOT  WHO  YOU  ARE WHO  ARE  YOU  WHO  WISHES  TO  STUDY  HERE" THE  MAN  WAS  GETTING  IRRITATED "I  AM,"  HE  STARTED,  BUT  HE  COULD  NOT  THINK  OF  ANYTHING  ELSE  TO  SAY,  SO  HE  TRAILED  OFF AFTER  A  LONG  PAUSE  THE  MASTER  REPLIED,  "THEN  YOU  ARE  WELCOME  TO  COME  STUDY" AN  INSTRUCTION DO  FOUR  UNREASONABLE  THINGS  EACH  DAY

## Contextual whole-section reading

Section spans: lp1-10, lp1-11, lp1-12, lp1-13

THE LOSS OF DIVINITY THE CIRCUMFERENCE PRACTICES THREE BEHAVIORS WHICH CAUSE THE LOSS OF DIVINITY CONSUMPTION WE CONSUME TOO MUCH BECAUSE WE BELIEVE THE FOLLOWING TWO ERRORS WITHIN THE DECEPTION 1 WE DO NOT HAVE ENOUGH, OR THERE IS NOT ENOUGH 2 WE HAVE WHAT WE HAVE NOW BY LUCK; AND WE WILL NOT BE STRONG ENOUGH LATER TO OBTAIN WHAT WE NEED MOST THINGS ARE NOT WORTH CONSUMING PRESERVATION WE PRESERVE THINGS BECAUSE WE BELIEVE WE ARE WEAK IF WE LOSE THEM WE WILL NOT BE STRONG ENOUGH TO GAIN THEM AGAIN THIS IS THE DECEPTION MOST THINGS ARE NOT WORTH PRESERVING ADHERENCE WE FOLLOW DOGMA SO THAT WE CAN BELONG AND BE RIGHT; OR WE FOLLOW REASON SO WE CAN BELONG AND BE RIGHT THERE IS NOTHING TO BE RIGHT ABOUT; TO BELONG IS DEATH IT IS THE BEHAVIORS OF CONSUMPTION, PRESERVATION AND ADHERENCE THAT HAVE US LOSE OUR PRIMALITY, AND THUS OUR DIVINITY SOME WISDOM AMASS GREAT WEALTH NEVER BECOME ATTACHED TO WHAT YOU OWN BE PREPARED TO DESTROY ALL THAT YOU OWN AN INSTRUCTION PROGRAM YOUR MIND PROGRAM REALITY

THE LOSS OF DIVINITY THE CIRCUMFERENCE PRACTICES THREE BEHAVIORS WHICH CAUSE THE LOSS OF DIVINITY CONSUMPTION WE CONSUME TOO MUCH BECAUSE WE BELIEVE THE FOLLOWING TWO ERRORS WITHIN THE DECEPTION 1 WE DO NOT HAVE ENOUGH, OR THERE IS NOT ENOUGH 2 WE HAVE WHAT WE HAVE NOW BY LUCK; AND WE WILL NOT BE STRONG ENOUGH LATER TO OBTAIN WHAT WE NEED MOST THINGS ARE NOT WORTH CONSUMING PRESERVATION WE PRESERVE THINGS BECAUSE WE BELIEVE WE ARE WEAK IF WE LOSE THEM WE WILL NOT BE STRONG ENOUGH TO GAIN THEM AGAIN THIS IS THE DECEPTION MOST THINGS ARE NOT WORTH PRESERVING ADHERENCE WE FOLLOW DOGMA SO THAT WE CAN BELONG AND BE RIGHT; OR WE FOLLOW REASON SO WE CAN BELONG AND BE RIGHT THERE IS NOTHING TO BE RIGHT ABOUT; TO BELONG IS DEATH IT IS THE BEHAVIORS OF CONSUMPTION, PRESERVATION AND ADHERENCE THAT HAVE US LOSE OUR PRIMALITY, AND THUS OUR DIVINITY SOME WISDOM AMASS GREAT WEALTH NEVER BECOME ATTACHED TO WHAT YOU OWN BE PREPARED TO DESTROY ALL THAT YOU OWN AN INSTRUCTION PROGRAM YOUR MIND PROGRAM REALITY

## Contextual whole-section reading

A  KOAN DURING  A  LESSON,  THE  MASTER  EXPLAINED  THE  I "THE  I  IS  THE  VOICE  OF  THE  CIRCUMFERENCE,"  HE  SAID WHEN  ASKED  BY  A  STUDENT  TO  EXPLAIN  WHAT  THAT  MEANT;  THE  MASTER  SAID  "IT  IS  A  VOICE  INSIDE  YOUR  HEAD" "I  DON'T  HAVE  A  VOICE  IN  MY  HEAD,"  THOUGHT  THE  STUDENT,  AND  HE  RAISED  HIS  HAND  TO  TELL  THE  MASTER THE  MASTER  STOPPED  THE  STUDENT,  AND  SAID  "THE  VOICE  THAT  JUST  SAID  YOU  HAVE  NO  VOICE  IN  YOUR  HEAD;  IS  THE  I" AND  THE  STUDENTS  WERE  ENLIGHTENED

ᚷᚾ-ᛄᛚᚳᚱ.ᛝᚣᛉᛋᚪᛟᚱᛉᚳ-ᛒᚫ-ᚠᚢᚪᛖᚪᚹ-/
ᛚᚾ-ᛄᛉ-ᚻᚦᛉ-ᛗᛚᚾᛖ-ᛏᛝᚦᚪᚩᚢᛗᚣ-ᚠᛝᚪ-/
ᚻᛡᛇᛡ-ᛚᛏᛁ-ᛇᛁ-ᚳᚢᚢᛖ-ᚳᛒ-ᚫᛇᚠᚦᚳᛚᚩᛉᛚ/
ᚩᛚ-ᚠᚳᛠ-ᚪᚠᛟᚫᚠ-ᚾᚳ-ᚢᛒᚱ-ᚾᛇᚩᛉ-ᛁᚳᛟ-ᛞ/
ᛉᛠᛝᚠᚱᛡᚳᛇ-ᛉᛟᛈᛗᛞᚳᚦᚹᛈ.ᛡᚻ-ᚾᚦ/
ᛇᛏᚹᛖᚢ-ᚫᛇᚦ-ᛝᛟᛏᚳᚷᛒᛠ-ᚪᚳᛒᚪᚩᚹᚫ-ᛉ/
ᚢ-ᚫᛖᛒ.ᛇᛏᚢᚩ-ᛟᛞᚠᚢᛋ.ᛡᛄᛗᚦᛠᛏᚪ-ᛒ/
ᚹᚣ-ᛏᛄᚻᚦᚫ-ᛚᚪᚱᚫᛟᚦᚩᚾᛟᛁᛖ-ᛡᚠᚷ-ᛋᚠᚦᛏ-/

## Visual observations

Decimal panel: Sixteen decimal numbers appear in four rows and four columns. 3299 is the only red entry; 708 is the only three-digit entry.

Open-loop drawing: Below the number panel are two open lobes with a crossing, resembling an infinity sign. Visible gaps remain in the drawing. Its intended meaning is not established.

Header: The red header contains nine runes in groups of four and five: F U L M / A EA Y OE A. Latin labels are transliterations, not plaintext.

3278 3299 3298 2838

## Archived transcription

ᛖᛞᚪᚫᛏᚩᛠᛖᛠᛉᚳᛠᛏ-ᚩᛞᚳᛠᚾᚳᚦ/
ᛗ-ᛞ-ᚷᛁᚳᚹᛟ-ᚪᚢᛒᚳᚫ-ᚦᚱ-ᛋᚣᚪ-ᛏᚦᛒ-ᛝᚹᛋᚱᛁ/

ᛁ-ᛞᛡᛄᚪᛈᚱᛋ-ᚢᛡ-ᚻᚷ-ᛚᛟᚠ-ᚻᚷᚫᛋ.ᛈᚹᚷᚷ/

ᛄᚳᚣ-ᚢᛄᚦᛄᚪᚾᛏᛒ-ᚳᛈᛡᛄᛋᚫ-ᛋᛗ-ᚻᛞᛠ/
ᛉᚢᛗ-ᛏᛠᛖᚣᚠ-ᛄᛏᛋᛗᛞᛟᛁᛝᚪᛉᛖᛈ-ᛚ/

ᚳᛁᛒᛈᚫ-ᚣᛖᛄᛝ-ᛞᚢᚱ-ᛉᛟᚩ-ᚠᚹᚩ-ᚣᛁᚠᚢᛇ-ᛚ/
ᛏᛈᛒᛗ-ᛇᛝ-ᚢᚳᚱᛡ-ᛖᚩᛁᚣᛄᛏᛡ-ᛖᚠᛇᚠᛚ-ᛁ/
.ᚣᚷᚠᛝᛡᛈᚷᛒ-ᛡᚩᚷᛡ-ᛟᚾᚹᛡᛈᛟ-ᚦᛈ-ᛟᚷ/

ᛝᛏᚳᚪ-ᛠᚣᚷ-ᚳᚦᛖᚾᚢᛁᚫᛁᚢᛡ-ᚹᛚᚳ-ᚻᛈ-ᛞ/
ᛄᚳ-ᛗᛒ-ᛗᚪᛄ-ᚩᚪᛞᛁ-ᚩᚱᛟᚠᛖᚣᛟᛁ.ᛇᛟ-ᛁᛈᚣ/
ᛚᚪᛡ-ᚳᛏᛠᛋᛖᛒᛝ-ᚫᛟᚫᛞᛖᛞᚣᛡ-ᛠᚪᛖ/
ᚦᛚᚫ-ᚳᛋᚪᚩᚷᚹᛚ.ᛈᛖ'ᛏ-ᛄᛉᛝᛚ-ᛏᛉᚩᚣᛝ/
ᚠᚩᚣ-ᛁᚻ-ᛟᚫᚷᛄᛝᛡᚾᛗᚣᛟᛡ-ᛝᚷᛖᛉ-ᛟᛉ/
ᛈᛚᛋᛉᛠ-ᛚᛡ-ᚱᚪᛞ-ᛠᚷ-ᚱ-ᚳᛇᚻ-ᛗᚪᛟᚷ-/
ᛞᚪᛋᛡᚻ-ᛈᚷᛖᚳᛟᚱᛟᚢ-ᛁᚫᛟᚦ-ᛄᚱᛡ-ᚱᛖᚦ/
ᚣᛏᛝᛡᚩᛒ-ᛏᚦᚳ-ᛉᚳ-ᛋᚪᚫ-ᛗᚠᛄᚱᛖ-ᛡᛇᛁᛇ/
ᛟᛉᚳᚹᚪᛖ-ᛋᚢᛉ-ᛋᛟᛚ-ᛄᚾ-ᛈᛇᛒ-ᚦᚦ-ᛁᚫᛚᛋᛝ/
ᛄᛄᛡ-ᛟᚻᛇᚢᛚ-ᛁᚱ-ᛡᚻᛚᛏᚹᛉᛇ-ᚱᛏᛠ-ᛁᚫᛚ/
ᛗ-ᛁᚱᚷᛏᛠ-ᛇᛟᚻᛟᚳᛋᛏᚾᚩ-ᛁᚱᚷ-ᚹ-ᛞᚢᚣᛚᛁ/
ᛗᛒᚢ-ᛚᚱ-ᛏᛁᚢ-ᚷᚳᚠᛇ-ᛚᛇᚣᛏ-ᛏᚫᚢ-ᚫᛠᛇ/

## Archived transcription

ᚣᚾ-ᚢᚹᛝᚻ-ᚷᚣᚱ-ᚩᛁ-ᛚᚾᛉ-ᚾᚩᛈ-ᚠᛠᚫᚫᚩ-ᛉ/
ᚾᛋᛟᚫᛚ-ᚾᚫ-ᚦᚢᛠᚣᚫ-ᛈᛁᛇᚢᚱᛄ-ᛈᛟᛄᚪᛝᛈ/
ᚦᛈᚪᛝ-ᚣᛗᛟ-ᛉᛒᚢᛏᛇᛗᛈᚫᚣ-ᛉᚫᚣᚱᚫᚣ/
ᚠᚠᛗᛡ-ᛉᛖ-ᚱᚢᛏᚷᚢᚣᚱ-ᛡᚢᚩᛇᛁ-ᛄᚠᛈᛄ/
ᛞ-ᛁᚦᚩᚻᛡᚷᚻ./
1-ᛚᚦᛇᛟ-ᚪᚫᛠ-ᛗᛉᚻᚳᛉᚪᛏᚦ-ᚫᛉ-ᚩᛋᚳᛞ/
ᛏ-ᚣᚹᚾ-ᛟᛏᛉ-ᚹᛁᛟᛄᚠᛁᚩ-ᛁᚱᛋ-ᛉᚾᛗᚪᛡ-ᚱᛈᛋ/
ᛞ-ᛁᛟ-ᚻᛖᛏᚢᚹ-ᛠᛟᛞᛟᛄᛁᛝᛡ-ᛄᚱᛞᛗᛒ-ᚩ/
ᚳᚩ-ᚦᛟᚱᚢᛚ-ᚢᚦᛋᚢᛞᛚ-ᚷᛁᚣᛝᚩᛟ-ᛁᛖᚣ-ᛖᚠ-/
ᛇᛝᛒᛚᛁᚢᚣᚠᛟᚾᛟ-ᛒᛟᚷᛄᚪᚾᛗᚫ-ᚣᚦᚠ-ᛁᛒᛝᛈ/
ᚾᛁᚱᚷ-ᛄᛇᚫ-ᚻᚪ-ᚱᛉᛉ-ᚩᛚᚾᚫ-ᛞᚣᛒᚾᚪ./

Liberpedia / Reference
Gematria Primus

Alphabet reference · 29 symbols

The alphabet assigns a Latin label and a prime number to each of 29 runes. A zero-based index is useful for describing the order of the alphabet, but it is a different quantity from the prime value.

For example, ᚠ has index 0, Latin label F, and prime value 2. Labels such as TH and NG represent a single rune, not two symbols.

Rune	Latin label	Index (0–28)	Prime value	Aliases
ᚠ	F	0	2	F
ᚢ	U	1	3	U
ᚦ	TH	2	5	TH
ᚩ	O	3	7	O
ᚱ	R	4	11	R
ᚳ	C	5	13	C, K
ᚷ	G	6	17	G
ᚹ	W	7	19	W
ᚻ	H	8	23	H
ᚾ	N	9	29	N
ᛁ	I	10	31	I
ᛄ	J	11	37	J
ᛇ	EO	12	41	EO
ᛈ	P	13	43	P
ᛉ	X	14	47	X
ᛋ	S	15	53	S, Z
ᛏ	T	16	59	T
ᛒ	B	17	61	B
ᛖ	E	18	67	E
ᛗ	M	19	71	M
ᛚ	L	20	73	L
ᛝ	NG	21	79	NG, ING
ᛟ	OE	22	83	OE
ᛞ	D	23	89	D
ᚪ	A	24	97	A
ᚫ	AE	25	101	AE
ᚣ	Y	26	103	Y
ᛡ	IA	27	107	IA, IO
ᛠ	EA	28	109	EA
Reading the labels

Latin labels are transcription conventions. They do not, by themselves, decrypt the text. U/V and C/K may be represented differently in a contextual English reading. Keep the rune sequence available when comparing such readings.

Source: archived Gematria Primus chart · community reference.

Liberpedia / Reference
Transcription guide

Numbering, symbols, and editorial conventions

Page identifiers

LP1 contains pages 00–16; LP2 contains pages 00–57. These numbers identify the order in the public archive. They are not page numbers printed on every manuscript image. Use the release prefix when citing a page.

Three different representations
Original image: the preserved JPEG, including artwork, color, placement, and punctuation.
Archived transcription: a community-created symbolic representation of that image.
Known reading: a documented decoded or readable interpretation, shown separately when available.

Transcriptions cannot preserve every visual distinction. A delimiter in the text is not automatically proof of a particular printed mark or grammatical meaning.

Archive delimiter notation
Notation	Archive convention
-	Word separator
,	Three-dot symbol
.	Clause separator
&	Paragraph separator
$	Segment separator
§	Chapter separator
/	Line boundary
%	Page boundary

These names describe the transcription convention, not an independently established cipher function.

Corrections and measurements

The page record retains the archived text. Where a documented visual review identifies a correction, the record lists it explicitly and offers a separate reviewed-text view. Character offsets are zero-based positions in the archived Unicode text.

Rune counts and prime-value sums are calculated from the archived rune sequence. Decimal digits and punctuation do not contribute to these sums. Such totals describe the transcription; they are not proposed cipher keys.

Image coordinates

Recorded regions use the original JPEG pixels: x and y begin at the upper-left corner. Each rectangle is written as x, y, width, height. Cropped thumbnails are browsing aids; the full original and its checksum remain available.

Liberpedia · Sources & provenance · Source snapshot: 5 October 2026

Known readings

A Warning	LP1–01	atbash
Method, key, and counting conventions

p = 28 − c. Here c and p are zero-based rune indices in the 29-symbol alphabet.

Archived walkthrough · Recorded parameters and provenance


Welcome, Pilgrim	LP1–03 · LP1–04	vigenere
Method, key, and counting conventions

p = (c − key[j mod key length]) mod 29. Here c and p are zero-based rune indices in the 29-symbol alphabet.

Key indices: 23, 10, 1, 10, 9, 10, 16, 26
Literal key labels: DIUINITY.

The sequence starts at position 0. Continue the sequence across the listed pages in order. Non-rune characters do not advance the sequence.

Copy the runes at these zero-based positions without advancing the sequence: 48, 74, 84, 132, 159, 160, 250, 421, 443, 465, 514. Positions count runes across the listed section, excluding punctuation and decimal digits.

These positions were aligned to known readings. They do not establish a rule to skip every F or apply the same interruptions to unsolved pages.

The deep-web page reference	LP2–56	prime-minus-one
Method, key, and counting conventions

p = (c − (prime[j] − 1)) mod 29. Here c and p are zero-based rune indices in the 29-symbol alphabet.

The sequence starts at position 0. Prime position 0 is 2; subsequent primes are 3, 5, 7, and so on. The sequence resets at the page boundary. Non-rune characters do not advance the sequence.

Copy the runes at these zero-based positions without advancing the sequence: 56. Positions count runes across the listed section, excluding punctuation and decimal digits.

These positions were aligned to known readings. They do not establish a rule to skip every F or apply the same interruptions to unsolved pages.

Archived walkthrough · Recorded parameters and provenance


Parable	LP2–57	direct
Method, key, and counting conventions

p = c. Here c and p are zero-based rune indices in the 29-symbol alphabet.

Archived walkthrough · Recorded parameters and provenance

Before comparing spellings

Latin labels can use U for V and C for K, while a single rune may represent several Latin letters. These conventions can make a literal reading look unusual. Use the alphabet reference and preserve the underlying rune sequence.

The LP1-10 I/E correction is a documented transcription issue. It is shown beside the archived text instead of being silently replaced.

Evidence distinctions
Record	What it establishes
Original-format image	The preserved appearance and bytes of a public archive artifact.
Community transcription	A readable representation to inspect against the image; transcription mistakes remain possible.
Recorded visual observation	A specific inspection or measurement, limited to its stated region.
Known reading	An established reading from the archived solution record, distinct from raw rune labels.

Liberpedia / Reference
Spelling, rune choices, and prime sums

Exact arithmetic · Source spellings · What the numerical patterns establish

The exact rune sequence determines the number. A polished English rendering can conceal numerical structure by changing how several letters are represented. Some unusual spellings have numerical consequences; others are aliases, reorderings, or transcription errors.

The strongest example here is LP2-57: each of its three body sentences has a prime sum that reverses to another prime. We can verify that property. Whether each individual spelling was chosen specifically to produce it is a separate question.

1. Define the sum before interpreting it

For rune sequence r₁, …, rₙ, use S = GP(r₁) + … + GP(rₙ), where GP is the rune’s prime value in Gematria Primus. Count each rune once. These calculations exclude punctuation, spaces, line markers, and decimal digits.

Keep three choices explicit: which text (ciphertext or known decoded text), which boundary (word, sentence, or page), and which encoding (one multi-letter rune or several individual runes). Changing a choice changes the question being answered.

All examples below use the known decoded rune sequence. LP2-57 and LP1-16 are directly readable; WIDSOM on LP1-04 is taken from its documented keyed reading. The ordinary page sidebar’s prime sum instead describes the archived rune sequence.

2. LP2-57: sentence sums and emirps

An emirp is a prime whose decimal reversal is a different prime. The three body sentences, using the archive’s clause boundaries, have this property:

Text segment	Rune sum	Decimal reversal	Result
PARABLE — heading	449	944	449 is prime; 944 is composite
Like the instar tunneling to the surface.	1259	9521	Both prime; emirp
We must shed our own circumferences.	1031	1301	Both prime; emirp
Find the divinity within and emerge.	1229	9221	Both prime; emirp

The complete heading-plus-body total is 3968 = 2⁷ × 31, which is composite. “All numbers are prime” is therefore too broad. The boundary is part of the observation: the three body sentence sums are emirps; the whole-page sum is not prime.

Inspect every rune value in these four sums
PARABLE

ᛈᚪᚱᚪᛒᛚᛖ

43 + 97 + 11 + 97 + 61 + 73 + 67 = 449

LICE-THE-INSTAR-TUNNELNG-TO-THE-SURFACE

ᛚᛁᚳᛖᚦᛖᛁᚾᛋᛏᚪᚱᛏᚢᚾᚾᛖᛚᛝᛏᚩᚦᛖᛋᚢᚱᚠᚪᚳᛖ

73 + 31 + 13 + 67 + 5 + 67 + 31 + 29 + 53 + 59 + 97 + 11 + 59 + 3 + 29 + 29 + 67 + 73 + 79 + 59 + 7 + 5 + 67 + 53 + 3 + 11 + 2 + 97 + 13 + 67 = 1259

WE-MUST-SHED-OUR-OWN-CIRCUMFERENCES

ᚹᛖᛗᚢᛋᛏᛋᚻᛖᛞᚩᚢᚱᚩᚹᚾᚳᛁᚱᚳᚢᛗᚠᛖᚱᛖᚾᚳᛖᛋ

19 + 67 + 71 + 3 + 53 + 59 + 53 + 23 + 67 + 89 + 7 + 3 + 11 + 7 + 19 + 29 + 13 + 31 + 11 + 13 + 3 + 71 + 2 + 67 + 11 + 67 + 29 + 13 + 67 + 53 = 1031

FIND-THE-DIUINITY-WITHIN-AND-EMERGE

ᚠᛁᚾᛞᚦᛖᛞᛁᚢᛁᚾᛁᛏᚣᚹᛁᚦᛁᚾᚪᚾᛞᛖᛗᛖᚱᚷᛖ

2 + 31 + 29 + 89 + 5 + 67 + 89 + 31 + 3 + 31 + 29 + 31 + 59 + 103 + 19 + 31 + 5 + 31 + 29 + 97 + 29 + 89 + 67 + 71 + 67 + 11 + 17 + 67 = 1229

Why expanding the English spelling changes the result

The “NG” rune can stand for NG or ING. In the archived direct reading, TUNNELNG corresponds to contextual English “tunneling.” Adding an I rune when re-encoding that English word adds 31. Keeping everything else fixed changes the first sentence from 1259 to 1290 = 2 × 3 × 5 × 43. The emirp property disappears.

This gives a concrete numerical reason to preserve the original encoding. It does not make the NG/ING alias a spelling mistake: one rune legitimately represents several Latin letters. Inspect the original sequence.

3. Work through the spellings individually
Literal labels	Exact rune values	Sum	Source
CWESTIAN
ᚳᚹᛖᛋᛏᛡᚾ	13 + 19 + 67 + 53 + 59 + 107 + 29	347

Prime
	LP1-16
WIDSOM
ᚹᛁᛞᛋᚩᛗ	19 + 31 + 89 + 53 + 7 + 71	270

Composite
	LP1-04
BELIEUE
ᛒᛖᛚᛁᛖᚢᛖ	61 + 67 + 73 + 31 + 67 + 3 + 67	369

Composite
	LP1-10
FUNCTIAN
ᚠᚢᚾᚳᛏᛡᚾ	2 + 3 + 29 + 13 + 59 + 107 + 29	242

Composite
	LP1-05
ILLUSIANS
ᛁᛚᛚᚢᛋᛡᚾᛋ	31 + 73 + 73 + 3 + 53 + 107 + 29 + 53	422

Composite
	LP1-03
SUFFERNG
ᛋᚢᚠᚠᛖᚱᛝ	53 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 67 + 11 + 79	217

Composite
	LP1-03
CWESTIAN / KWESTION: the exact encoding matters

The seven labels are C · W · E · S · T · IA · N. C/K and IA/IO are alternative Latin labels for the same runes, so CWESTIAN and KWESTION can describe the same rune sequence. Its sum is 13 + 19 + 67 + 53 + 59 + 107 + 29 = 347, a prime.

For an explicit comparison, keep C W E S T and N fixed, but replace the single IA/IO rune (107) with separate I and O runes (31 + 7). The total becomes 347 − 107 + 31 + 7 = 278 = 2 × 139. This alternate rune encoding is composite. It is a counterfactual comparison, not text found on the page.

The conventional spelling QUESTION cannot be assigned a unique GP sum without an additional spelling rule: the chart has no separate Q rune. Quietly converting Q into some preferred sequence would build an assumption into the result. We can establish the printed encoding’s prime sum without claiming that this proves why the author selected it.

WIDSOM / WISDOM: reordering cannot tune an additive sum

Both use the same six rune values and sum to 270 = 2 × 3³ × 5. Swapping D and S changes their order, not their sum. The same holds for every larger word or sentence total containing that swap while keeping its boundary fixed.

Formally, for any permutation π, Σ GP(rᵢ) = Σ GP(rπ(i)). An order-sensitive cipher can distinguish the spellings; an additive prime sum cannot. WIDSOM is preserved in the known keyed reading of LP1-04, while WISDOM appears in LP1-05. Neither word total is prime.

If a calculation adds a delimiter value of 1, then 270 + 1 = 271, which is prime. That is a different counting convention, and it gives the same result for both word orders. The rune-only chart does not supply this extra 1. A punctuation-inclusive claim must state and justify its delimiter rule rather than quietly add it after seeing the total.

BELIEUE / BELEIUE: a transcription correction, not prime fitting

The native-image correction on LP1-10 restores BELIEUE from the archived I/E reversal. Both orders sum to 369 = 3² × 41. The correction matters for fidelity and sequence-sensitive work, but it cannot make an unchanged additive word or sentence sum prime. The U/V rendering in contextual BELIEVE does not add another rune.

FUNCTIAN, ILLUSIANS, SUFFERNG: aliases can look like omissions

IA/IO and NG/ING account for these literal forms. Their rune sums are 242, 422, and 217, all composite. Replacing IA/IO with separate I and O decreases the first two sums by 69, producing 173 and 353, both prime. Adding I before NG in SUFFERNG produces 248, composite.

These contrasting examples matter: the observed spelling does not universally maximize word-level primality. A claim about “fitting the primes” must name the intended boundary and evaluate the complete specified set, including examples that do not fit.

4. What can we say about purpose?

Established numerical property: the three LP2-57 body sentences have emirp sums under the stated rune-only convention. CWESTIAN’s recorded rune sequence has a prime word sum. The calculations are reproducible.

Numerical consequence: some plausible alternative encodings change these properties. Pure reorderings and alias relabelings leave additive sums unchanged. Transcription mistakes must be corrected from source evidence, not selected to improve a number.

Proposed purpose: exact wording and rune choices may have been constrained to produce particular totals, possibly as structural markers or consistency checks. These are interpretations of the pattern, not an authenticated explanation of intent. The known text’s statements about sacred primes provide relevant context, but do not specify a universal spelling-selection rule.

A useful test fixes the target unit, segmentation, punctuation values, and allowed alternatives before counting. Count all matches and non-matches. Searching many boundaries, aliases, reversals, and offsets creates many opportunities to find a prime; a selected hit alone does not quantify how surprising it is. No calibrated probability of authorial intent is claimed here.

Reading the text
Do unusual spellings make the sums prime?

CWESTIAN totals 347, a prime. WIDSOM and WISDOM both total 270; BELIEUE and BELEIUE both total 369. Rune choices can change sums, while reordering the same runes cannot.

Start solving: a practical introduction

Find the right pages, reproduce known results, and turn an idea into a test someone else can repeat.

Liber Primus combines visible artwork, rune text, numbers, and hidden file content. Learn how these layers differ before treating them as one cipher. A title image can have no runic paragraph and still carry a signed OutGuess message.

1. Know the collection
The first release contains 17 images, including two title pages. The second release contains 58. In the archived source snapshot, LP1 has known readings and LP2 has readings for 56 and 57; LP2 pages 00–55 remain unsolved. This is dated documented knowledge, not live proof that nobody has solved anything else.
Use IDs such as LP2-31. “Page 31” without a release or archive name is ambiguous. The numbering cross-reference maps release IDs to archive filenames.

2. Reproduce one short reading
Open the warning in the reader. Compare the original image with its runes, then follow the complete warning reading and its Atbash explanation. Use the 29-symbol alphabet, not English A–Z. Count a multi-letter rune as one symbol.

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --check-all
Run these from a downloaded or cloned repository with Python 3. They use the standard library and make no AI requests. The first prints a literal reading; the second checks all 17 known runic-page outputs. Download the full repository from GitHub’s Code menu: the script needs its text and parameter files.

New to the terminal? Running the reproduction scripts walks through setup, expected results, trace columns, and common errors.
3. Learn the other layers
Rune indices and prime values: cipher arithmetic versus prime sums.
Vigenère: keys, direction, and continuity across pages.
The cover payload chain: OutGuess, hexadecimal, XOR, signatures, and transposition.
Spelling and prime sums: a reproducible numerical property versus an explanation of a spelling’s purpose.

For the ideas behind the decoded passages, start with philosophical themes, then compare the William Blake parallel. These guides distinguish the manuscript words, interpretation, and possible outside sources.

4. Make an idea testable
Choose a page, a region, a transformation, and a success criterion. “Try primes” is too broad. “Subtract consecutive prime-minus-one values modulo 29 from LP2-31, starting at the first rune, carrying through punctuation, with no skipped runes” specifies one test. It does not establish that this is the correct method.
Check Have we tried it? for the technique and scope. The registry is awaiting reviewed records; an empty result means no published match here, not that an idea is new. Follow the reproducibility guide.

Ready to contribute
You should be able to identify an exact image, distinguish raw from corrected transcription, reproduce a known reading, and explain what would count against your hypothesis. You do not need to understand every cipher before inspecting a well-defined detail.
For a worked descriptive analysis, use the index-of-coincidence baseline: exact rune counts, downloadable results, reproduction commands and the limits of frequency evidence.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

Running the reproduction scripts

Set up the repository, verify a known reading, understand a rune-by-rune trace, and diagnose common errors.

The reproduction scripts let you check a published reading against exact stored outputs. Start with the warning on LP1-01: it uses a short Atbash transformation and needs no external Python packages. These scripts reproduce documented controls; they do not search for new solutions.

1. Get the whole repository

Open the Liberpedia repository, choose Code → Download ZIP, and extract it. Open the extracted folder containing scripts, text, and data. An image bundle or an individually downloaded script is not enough: the reading script also needs the archived transcriptions, method parameters, and expected readings.

Alternatively, clone the repository if you already use Git:

git clone https://github.com/jelliottdev/jelliottdev.github.io.git
cd jelliottdev.github.io

Open a terminal in that folder. On Windows, File Explorer’s “Open in Terminal” command can open the selected folder. The commands below assume this working directory. If your path contains spaces, put quotation marks around it when using cd.

2. Check Python

You need Python 3. On Windows, try py --version; on macOS or Linux, try python3 --version. If neither command is available, install Python from the official Python downloads or your operating system’s package manager, then reopen your terminal. A command that prints a Python 2 version is not suitable.

	Terminal	First control
	Windows PowerShell	py scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
	macOS / Linux	python3 scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
	If python already selects Python 3	python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning

The wiki’s other recipes use python as shorthand. Substitute the command that worked on your machine; the script path and arguments stay the same. No API key, model download, or hosted AI request is involved.

3. Check the expected result

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --list
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --check-all

--list prints nine named section controls. warning prints === LP1-01 === followed by its literal reading, after checking it against the stored page output. --check-all should finish with:

PASS: 17 literal page readings match the published controls exactly.

Nine sections and 17 pages are different counts: several sections span multiple images. This check covers the known runic-page outputs in the repository, not all 75 images, their hidden payloads, or unsolved ciphertext. The complete warning guide shows both the literal output and contextual English. Do not normalize spellings before comparing literal outputs.

4. Read a rune-by-rune trace

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --trace

The output is CSV: one row per recognized rune, with a header naming each field. The first two rows are:

page,page_rune_ordinal,section_rune_ordinal,input_rune,input_index,subtracted_value,output_index,latin,copied
lp1-01,0,0,ᚱ,4,,24,A,False
lp1-01,1,1,ᛝ,21,,7,W,False

Atbash maps index x to 28 − x. The first rune has index 4, so its output index is 24, labeled A. The second has index 21, so its output is 7, labeled W. These are zero-based alphabet indices, not prime values. A two-letter Latin label such as NG still represents one rune.

	Field	Meaning

	page_rune_ordinal	Zero-based rune position within the page; resets at each new page.

	section_rune_ordinal	Position under the control’s section/boundary rule. It can continue across pages.

	input_index, output_index	Positions in the 29-rune alphabet before and after the transformation.

	subtracted_value	The applied Vigenère or prime-minus-one amount. Blank for Atbash, direct reading, or a copied interruption; blank is not a recorded zero.

	latin	The output rune’s Latin label, before contextual English editing.

	copied	Whether this position is listed as an interruption in the control. False does not mean the index changed: direct readings also have false entries.


Non-rune characters are preserved in the literal output but do not get trace rows. For a key-dependent example, run python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome --trace and follow keystream positions and interruptions. The specific LP1-10 correction is applied before transformation and trace output; see transcription layers.

Which tools need extra software?

	Task	Requirements	Instructions

	Known rune readings	Python 3, standard library only	Warning control

	Reconstruct the exported cover chain	Python 3, standard library only; uses stored extractions	Cover chain

	Check visual-record structure	Python 3, standard library only	Opening-page inventory

	Recount image pixels with --pixels	Python 3 and Pillow	Image regions and measurement rules

	Extract hidden JPEG payloads again	Python wrapper plus an OutGuess executable	OutGuess extraction

	Verify signed messages	GnuPG and the documented public key	PGP signatures


When a command fails

“Command not found” or “not recognized”: check the Python command first. If it names outguess or gpg, that is a separate executable, not a missing rune dataset.

“Can’t open file” for the script: check the terminal’s current folder. You need the extracted repository root, not its parent or the still-compressed ZIP.

A missing text/ or data/ file: obtain the complete repository. The script locates these directories relative to its own file.

Boxes instead of runes: the terminal font may lack runic characters. Check the numeric indices and Latin labels, and compare with the browser reader. Missing glyphs alone do not establish bad input bytes.

“Output differs” or a hash mismatch: preserve the full error and identify the affected file. Compare with an unchanged copy and the checksums. Do not change the expected output merely to make the check pass.

Keep the result reproducible

Record the repository commit, Python version, command, and output. In a Git checkout, git rev-parse HEAD prints the commit ID. For a ZIP download, retain the archive and its checksum; do not claim a commit ID you have not verified. When you move from a control to a new hypothesis, follow documenting a reproducible attempt. A passing control is a starting point, not evidence that the same method solves another page.

Reproducing rune prime sums provides a read-only command and explicit spelling comparisons.
Implementation and verification

The commands and trace fields above are documented from the reproduction script and its control parameters. The first trace rows and all 17 literal page outputs were checked locally on 19 October 2026. Operating-system launch commands are alternatives; this verification used Python 3.12 on Windows.

Transliteration and literal readings

Keep manuscript symbols separate from the decisions made while interpreting them.

Different text layers
A transcription records runes. A transliteration replaces each rune with a Latin label. A cipher transformation may produce plaintext rune indices, whose labels form a literal decoded reading. Contextual English can normalize spelling or interpret those labels. It is an editorial layer.
Transliterating encrypted runes does not decrypt them. Conversely, direct-reading sections need no nontrivial substitution.

Compare the right outputs
Begin with the image and archived rune text. Record corrections before applying a cipher. Compare a literal output with the page-level control, not a normalized paragraph spanning several pages. Preserve spelling when testing prime sums.
On LP1-10, a documented I/E order correction matters. The script swaps runes at zero-based ordinals 116 and 117; it does not rewrite every similar sequence. See the transcription guide.
The worked trace guide follows the first two warning runes from input indices to literal labels.

Documenting a reproducible attempt

Make the question, inputs, transformations, and limits checkable.

Define the claim
Name page IDs, regions, input hashes, transcription versions, transformation order, key space, offsets, and boundary rules. State which parameters were fixed in advance and which were selected after viewing outputs.

Use known controls
A control has an expected result. Reproducing the warning checks an Atbash implementation; reproducing LP2-56 checks a particular prime schedule. One control does not validate every method or transcription.

For setup and a worked trace before writing your own attempt, see running the reproduction scripts.
What to record
The question and bounded tested scope.
Input paths, hashes, and explicit corrections.
A readable script, requirements, and copyable command.
Parameter bounds, random seeds, and candidate counts.
Expected and actual outputs, with the matching criterion.
What was not tested and what would change the conclusion.

Selection changes the evidence
Trying many spellings, boundaries, reversals and offsets creates opportunities for chance patterns. A probability claim must account for the selection process. A null model is the comparison process expected without the proposed mechanism; preserve relevant properties such as symbol counts or region lengths. There is no universal coincidence probability for an unspecified search.
Report “no match under these parameters,” not “the technique cannot work.” Label patterns selected after inspection as candidates for independent testing. See spelling and sums.

Worked distinctions: emirps and prime-index calculations.
The research registry
Have we tried it? compares techniques and scope in published records. Background pages do not count as experiments. The registry remains empty while records are prepared and retested. The contribution format describes publication requirements.
For a worked descriptive analysis, use the index-of-coincidence baseline: exact rune counts, downloadable results, reproduction commands and the limits of frequency evidence.

Rune indices and prime values

The same rune has an alphabet position and a separate Gematria Primus prime value.

Two mappings, two jobs
The alphabet has 29 symbols. Its zero-based indices run from 0 to 28. Its prime values are the first 29 primes, from 2 to 109. F has index 0 and prime value 2; U has index 1 and prime value 3; TH has index 2 and prime value 5.
Known substitution ciphers use indices modulo 29. A Gematria Primus sum adds the prime values. Replacing one operation with the other changes the hypothesis.

See prime values and prime indices for the indexing convention and larger-number examples.
Count symbols, not Latin characters
TH, EO, NG and other multi-letter labels each denote a single rune. U/V and C/K renderings also require the stated convention. Work from runes when computing sums and offsets.

Reproduce a small example
For F–U–TH, the indices are [0, 1, 2] and the prime sum is 2 + 3 + 5 = 10. Atbash transforms the indices to [28, 27, 26]; it does not reverse the digits of the sum.
Next: modular arithmetic, literal readings, and worked spelling sums.
Reproducing rune prime sums provides a read-only command and explicit spelling comparisons.

---

Arithmetic modulo 29

How shifts wrap around the rune alphabet, including negative results.

What “mod 29” means
Two integers are equal modulo 29 when their difference is a multiple of 29. For rune indices, choose the representative from 0 through 28. Moving forward from 28 by one returns to 0; moving backward from 0 by one returns to 28.

Worked steps
If ciphertext index c is 3 and the key value is 10, then p = (3 − 10) mod 29 = 22. Adding 29 to −7 gives the same index. A shift by 31 is equivalent to a shift by 2.
# Python:
assert (3 - 10) % 29 == 22
# JavaScript needs normalization of its signed remainder:
# ((3 - 10) % 29 + 29) % 29

What this does not decide
Modulo arithmetic supplies wraparound, not the key, direction, offset, or interruptions. See Vigenère, prime-minus-one, and keystream positions.

Atbash and shifted Atbash

Reverse the rune alphabet, with an extra shift where the control specifies one.

The mapping
Ordinary Atbash gives p = 28 − c. Index 0 maps to 28, 1 to 27, and 14 to itself. Applying it twice returns the original index. It reverses the alphabet mapping, not rune order within a line.
The warning uses ordinary Atbash. The first koan, LP1-06–09, uses p = (28 − c + 3) mod 29. For c = 0 this produces index 2, because 31 mod 29 = 2.

How to replicate
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py first-koan
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --trace
The trace exposes each rune’s operation and result. Punctuation remains in place. Compare with the exact controls and known readings.

What passing a control means
A matching output confirms that your convention reproduces that passage. It does not establish that an unsolved page uses Atbash. Keep ordinary and shifted variants distinct in a test record.

Vigenère on the rune alphabet

A repeating key supplies a shift at each consumed rune position.

Specify direction and key
This wiki uses p = (c − k[j mod L]) mod 29, where L is key length and j counts consumed key positions. The welcome uses [23, 10, 1, 10, 9, 10, 16, 26], labeled DIVINITY. The second koan has its own key and interruption list in the parameters.
A walkthrough may express decryption as addition of complementary values. Subtracting 23 modulo 29 equals adding 6. The same keyword with the wrong direction can produce the wrong result.

How to replicate
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome --trace
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py second-koan
Use the complete parameters. The welcome spans LP1-03–04 without resetting the key; the second koan spans LP1-14–15. Punctuation does not advance the key.

Interruptions affect alignment
Specified runes are copied without consuming a key value. These interruptions were aligned to known readings. They are not a rule to skip every F or permission to add skips until an output looks English.
If output matches until one point, inspect the trace around that point. Check transcription, multi-letter rune counting, boundary resets, and whether a copied rune consumed a key value. One alignment error can affect every later rune.

Keystream positions and interruptions

Which symbols consume the next key or prime value?

Keep separate counters
The rune ordinal identifies a rune in the input section. The keystream position identifies the next shift. Both normally advance for each rune. At a recorded interruption, the rune is copied and its ordinal advances, but the keystream does not.
Spaces, line breaks, punctuation and decimal digits do not consume rune positions in these controls. Position 56 means the 57th rune, not the 56th file character.

Recorded examples
The welcome list is [48, 74, 84, 132, 159, 160, 250, 421, 443, 465, 514] across its two pages. LP2-56 copies ordinal 56. The parameter file records all lists and whether sequences carry or reset at boundaries.

Inspect alignment
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome --trace
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-56 --trace
After a copied rune, the next transformed rune receives the unconsumed shift. See Vigenère and prime-minus-one.
No universal skip rule
A new skip list is an additional hypothesis. If chosen after viewing the output, disclose that choice and test its predictions on independent material.

Prime-minus-one decoding

Reproduce LP2-56 with a prime sequence and one recorded interruption.

The transformation
Take prime[j] from 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, … and compute p = (c − (prime[j] − 1)) mod 29. The first shifts are 1, 2, 4, 6, 10, …. This is not the prime value assigned to the ciphertext rune.
At j = 0, index 0 becomes 28; at j = 1, index 0 would become 27. These are arithmetic examples, not assertions about the page’s first two runes.

The historical name φ(prime), or Euler’s totient of a prime, gives exactly these shifts.
How to replicate LP2-56
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-56
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-56 --trace
Start at prime 2. Copy zero-based rune ordinal 56 without advancing the prime sequence. Preserve punctuation. Compare with the literal reading.

The hash reference
The decoded text refers to a page identified by a long hash. Reproducing that text is not the same as locating the referenced page. See the exact hash target and its unresolved input conventions.

Euler’s totient and prime-minus-one

Why φ(p) equals p − 1 for primes, and what that means for LP2-56.

Euler’s totient function, written φ(n), counts the integers from 1 through n that are relatively prime to n. Two integers are relatively prime when their greatest common divisor is 1. “Relatively prime” does not mean that both integers are themselves prime.

Small examples
For n = 8, the qualifying integers are 1, 3, 5, and 7, so φ(8) = 4. For a prime p, every integer from 1 through p − 1 is relatively prime to p. Therefore φ(p) = p − 1. In particular, φ(2), φ(3), φ(5), φ(7) are 1, 2, 4, 6.

Why the LP2-56 method has two names
The archived walkthrough describes LP2-56 using “phi(prime).” The prime-minus-one guide uses the equivalent expression p − 1. These are the same shifts when the input sequence consists of primes. Substituting φ(n) for consecutive integers n would produce a different sequence.

How to reproduce the identity
from math import gcd
def phi(n):
    return sum(gcd(k, n) == 1 for k in range(1, n + 1))
assert phi(8) == 4
assert [phi(p) for p in [2, 3, 5, 7]] == [1, 2, 4, 6]
This deliberately simple implementation is useful for small examples. Reproduce the actual page with python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-56, including its recorded interruption and modulo-29 arithmetic.

What the identity does not determine
It does not specify the starting prime, direction, reset behavior, or copied rune positions. Those parameters remain part of the keystream convention.

Sources
Pinned LP2-56 walkthrough · Exact reproduction parameters.

Transposition ciphers

Reorder symbols without substituting their values.

Preserve symbols, change positions
A permutation uses every position once, preserving length and symbol counts. Atbash and Vigenère change values; a pure transposition does not.

The historical column operation
Set rows to the five strings in the cover-chain grid:
order = [2, 8, 9, 1, 12, 13, 11, 4, 5, 7, 3, 0, 6, 10]
assert sorted(order) == list(range(14))
assert len(rows) == 5 and all(len(row) == 14 for row in rows)
result = "".join(rows[r][c] for r in range(5) for c in order)

Define the search space
Record grid dimensions, fill and read directions, padding, and permutation. Fourteen columns admit 14! = 87,178,291,200 orders. A fragment selected after many choices needs stronger support than a prediction from an independently specified order. See controls and scope.

OutGuess extraction

Recover hidden bytes from the original JPEG before interpreting them.

Steganography, not a rune cipher
OutGuess retrieves data hidden in an image carrier. Resizing, resaving, screenshotting or recompressing a JPEG can change its bytes. Use the original JPEG, not a thumbnail.

How to replicate
Install or build OutGuess for your operating system. No executable is bundled here. From the repository root, use an executable on PATH or supply its path:
python scripts/extract_payload.py lp1-00 --outguess outguess --output cover.bin
The wrapper checks the image hash, retrieves the default-key payload, and checks its expected hash before writing a new file. It refuses to overwrite a destination. The underlying operation is:
outguess -r -k "Default key" images/lp1-00.jpg cover.bin
The cover’s full extraction is 2,899 bytes. Checksums and the exact verified build are in the manifest. Compare output bytes, not merely a success message.

Keep the layers separate
Preserve the full extraction. The exported signed block supports PGP verification; the body is a separate derivative. On the cover, that body is hexadecimal. Follow the three-image chain to interpret it.

Coverage and tool source
Eight documented extractions were reproduced on 19 October 2026. This does not rule out other keys or hiding methods. The upstream repository is archived, not actively maintained. Pinned source · Payload inventory.

Embedded OutGuess payloads

Eight LP1 images with reproduced extractions and verified signatures.

The visible manuscript and JPEG carrier have distinct layers. The cover and chapter-title images participate in a hidden-message chain.

Verified inventory
	Image	Bytes	Files	Provenance
	LP1-00	2,899	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
	LP1-01	2,899	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
	LP1-02	2,899	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
	LP1-03	31,809	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
	LP1-10	1,234	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
	LP1-11	1,234	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
	LP1-12	1,234	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
	LP1-13	1,234	Extraction · Signed block · Body	Source
Default-key extraction and signature checks were repeated on 19 October 2026. The manifest records hashes and verification modes. This positive inventory does not rule out other hidden data.

Cover, warning, and chapter title
LP1-00, LP1-01 and LP1-02 contain signed hex bodies. Decode and XOR them to recover another signed message. Follow the complete chain; examining one body alone misses that relationship.

Welcome: LP1-03
The body begins “Let the text guide you,” followed by a good-luck message and a hex-encoded JPEG. The embedded image is distinct from the visible manuscript image. Preserve the signed body separately from the decoded derivative. Full body.
JPEG decoded from the signed body; a derivative, not the carrier page.
Download the decoded JPEG (15,188 bytes). To reproduce it:
from pathlib import Path
body = Path("exports/steganography/lp1-03.body.txt").read_text()
image = bytes.fromhex(body[body.index("ffd8ffe"):])
with open("embedded.jpg", "xb") as f:
    f.write(image)
Read the embedded image’s transcription and reproduction guide.
LP1-10 through LP1-13
These historical instructions discuss a Tor hidden service, CGI uploads, three magic squares, and working alone. They are source documents, not current wiki setup instructions. Decorative borders use 3s on LP1-10 and LP1-11, 0s on LP1-12, and 1s on LP1-13. Similar prose does not make signed files byte-identical.

Magic squares: definitions, historical examples, and the payload number arrangement.
Reproduce, then interpret
Follow extraction, checksum verification, and signature verification as separate steps. This makes disagreements traceable to an operation and a file.

Hexadecimal and byte streams

An encoding of bytes, not by itself an encryption method.

Two digits per byte
Hexadecimal uses 0–9 and a–f for values 0–15. Each digit encodes four bits; two encode one byte. Hex 41 is decimal 65, the ASCII byte for A. Leading zeros matter.

Decode a cover body
from pathlib import Path
body = Path("exports/steganography/lp1-00.body.txt").read_text()
data = bytes.fromhex(body)
assert len(data) == 991
Whitespace may separate digits. Each of the first three bodies has 1,982 hex digits and decodes to 991 bytes. Those bytes need not be readable. The next step is bytewise XOR.

Do not decode prose as hex
LP1-03 contains prose followed by hex-encoded JPEG data. Isolate the hex portion before decoding and retain the complete signed body separately from the derivative image.

---

Exclusive OR (XOR)

The bitwise operation used to combine the three cover-chain payloads.

Exclusive OR, usually written XOR or ⊕, compares bits. Two equal bits give 0; two different bits give 1. Programming languages commonly use ^ for this operation on integers.

A byte example
00001111   (hex 0f)
00110011   (hex 33)
--------
00111100   (hex 3c)
XOR is not addition with carries and is not alphabet arithmetic modulo 29. It works independently at each bit position.

The three-image chain
The signed bodies from LP1-00, LP1-01, and LP1-02 are first decoded from hexadecimal. XOR their corresponding bytes to reconstruct a signed message. XORing their ASCII hex characters would be a different operation.

How to replicate
assert len(a) == len(b) == len(c)
combined = bytes(x ^ y ^ z for x, y, z in zip(a, b, c))
# Full checked reproduction:
# python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py
The length check prevents silent truncation by zip. Do not pad, cycle, or trim these documented inputs. Follow the complete recipe for the resulting signature and transposition.

Useful identities and their limits
A ⊕ A = 0 and A ⊕ 0 = A. Applying the same XOR mask twice recovers the input. The three inputs can be combined in any order because XOR is associative and commutative. Those identities explain the computation; they do not establish why a particular set of manuscript files should be combined.

Sources
Pinned 2014 walkthrough · Input and output hashes.

The cover payload chain

The cover, warning, and chapter title combine into a signed message and a transposition.

Three inputs
LP1-00, Liber Primus, LP1-01, the warning, and LP1-02, Chapter 1 — Intus carry OutGuess payloads. Extract and verify them. Their 1,982-digit bodies decode to three 991-byte streams.

Visible headings and the two title pages.
XOR corresponding bytes
What XOR means, with a worked byte example.
XOR produces a 0 bit when input bits agree and 1 when they differ. Compute result[i] = A[i] XOR B[i] XOR C[i] on decoded bytes, not on hexadecimal text characters. For example, 0x0f XOR 0x33 = 0x3c.
python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py
python scripts/reproduce_cover_chain.py --output combined.asc
The script checks input and output hashes and refuses to overwrite files. Its 991-byte result is another signed message, requiring its own signature check.

Read the columns
Remove spaces from the first two ciphertext lines and arrange the 70 characters in five rows of fourteen:
IDGTKUMLOOARWO
ERTHISUTETLHUT
IATSLLOUIMNITE
LNJ7TFYVOIUAUS
NOCO5JI4MEODZZ
Within each row, take columns in zero-based order 2, 8, 9, 1, 12, 13, 11, 4, 5, 7, 3, 0, 6, 10. Concatenate the five reordered rows from top to bottom. This transposition gives:
GOODWORKULTIMATETRUTHISTHEULTIMATEILLUSIONJOINUSATFV7LYUCMEOZZD5J4ONIO

Preserve the literal ending
The exact output ends in ONIO. The historical walkthrough restores a final N to render fv7lyucmeozzd5j4.onion. That character is an interpretation, not a permutation output. This is a historical address, not a claim of current reachability.
The supplied permutation reproduces the known result. It does not show that a unique ordering can be inferred without clues or applied to another page.

PGP signatures and the Cicada key

Verify archived messages and state what verification establishes.

Signature validity and identity
A valid signature ties a signed message to a key. It does not decrypt its body, sign every byte of the enclosing JPEG, or by itself identify a real-world author. Historical association with Cicada is a separate provenance claim.
The full primary fingerprint of the exported key is 6D854CD7933322A601C3286D181F01E57A35090F. Check the key itself, not its filename or short ID.

Verify in a separate keyring
Install GnuPG, create an empty directory named verify-keyring, and run from the repository root:
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --import exports/steganography/cicada-public-key.asc
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --fingerprint
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --verify exports/steganography/lp1-00.signed.asc
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --verify exports/steganography/cover-chain.signed.asc
Compare the full fingerprint. A good signature and unknown trust can coexist: validity differs from identity-trust assignments. No private key is required.

Read the verification output
For an inspectable status stream, add --status-fd 1:
gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --status-fd 1 --verify exports/steganography/lp1-00.signed.asc
The fresh isolated check produced these status types: GOODSIG, VALIDSIG and TRUST_UNDEFINED. The VALIDSIG line identified the full fingerprint above. The trust warning did not mean the signature failed: this new keyring contained no identity-trust assignments. Do not assign trust merely to silence that warning. GnuPG documents these machine-readable records in its status-format specification.
The displayed user ID, Cicada 3301 (845145127), is a label associated with the key; matching that text is not the same as matching the fingerprint. Keep the verification result, key provenance, and real-world identity claim separate.
If verification fails
No public key: confirm that you imported the shipped key into the same directory supplied to --homedir.
No signed data: check that you selected the preserved .signed.asc block, not the extracted body or decoded binary stream.
Bad signature: compare the file checksum with the manifest and obtain an unchanged copy before drawing conclusions.
Rejected digest: inspect the exact diagnostic and the compatibility note below; a policy rejection differs from a verified signature.
Legacy digest compatibility
Some versions reject historical SHA-1 signatures by policy. If that is the reported cause, repeat this isolated check with --allow-weak-digest-algos on that command only. Record the flag; do not change global settings or treat SHA-1 as suitable for new signatures.

The earlier extraction manifest records the compatibility mode used in that run. A fresh isolated check with GnuPG 2.5.21 on Windows, --no-options, and no compatibility override verified all eight extracted signed blocks plus the reconstructed cover-chain message. The nine-file verification record stores input hashes, status lines, options and version. Do not assume a flag is necessary simply because another verification run used it.
--homedir selects the separate keyring directory; --no-options avoids reading the default options file. See GnuPG configuration options and digest compatibility options.
Different files, different purposes
The manifest separately hashes full extractions, signed blocks, and bodies. Verifying an edited body is not equivalent to verifying the preserved signed block. See extraction and checksums.

File hashes and checksums

Identify exact bytes without confusing integrity, signatures, and decryption.

What a checksum establishes
SHA-256 maps bytes to a 256-bit digest, displayed as 64 hex digits. A matching digest identifies expected bytes under the hash’s security assumptions, not their creator. Changed line endings can change a text file’s hash.

Check a download
# PowerShell
Get-FileHash images/lp1-00.jpg -Algorithm SHA256
# Linux
sha256sum images/lp1-00.jpg
# macOS
shasum -a 256 images/lp1-00.jpg
Compare with the catalog or download entry. Hash the actual file, not its displayed preview.

LP2-56: exact target, algorithm assumptions, and input bytes.
The puzzle’s hash target
LP2-56 refers to a page identified by a hash. SHA-512 has 128 hexadecimal digits; it differs from this wiki’s SHA-256 distribution checksums. A hash is not normally reversible into its input. Candidate checks need the correct bytes and serialization.
See signatures for signed evidence and prime-minus-one for reproducing the text containing the target.

Prime values and prime indices

Distinguish a prime from its ordinal, and reproduce the 3299 and 9467 calculations.

A prime’s value and its position in the ordered list of primes are different numbers. Specify which operation you mean before combining a prime with a page number or rune value.

Value versus ordinal
Write pn for the nth prime, using one-based indexing: p1 = 2, p2 = 3, p3 = 5. Looking up p3299 gives 30,557. This means that 30,557 is the 3,299th prime; it does not mean that 3,299 has ordinal 30,557.
The rune alphabet instead uses zero-based positions 0–28. Rune index i has Gematria Primus value pi+1. Confusing these conventions introduces an off-by-one error.

The 3299 and 9467 examples
The decimal number 3299 appears in red on LP2-15. The arithmetic lookups p3299 = 30,557 and p9467 = 98,597 are exact. Their product is:
98597 × 30557 = 3012828529
 9857 × 30557 =  301200349
The second expression omits a 9 and gives a different answer. Preserve the operands as well as the final sequence when describing a hypothesis. These calculations establish arithmetic, not a relationship between manuscript pages.

LP2-15: the complete number panel, heading, and drawing.
How to replicate
python scripts/check_number_examples.py
The script enumerates primes by exact trial division and checks the examples. It makes no network calls or model requests. See emirps and reversal for a distinct operation, and documenting scope before proposing a decoding chain.

Sources
Original page and provenance · Arithmetic source code. Prime notation is a mathematical definition; the page’s printed number does not itself specify this lookup operation.

Emirps and decimal reversal

Check reversed primes without conflating reversal, mirroring, and prime lookup.

An emirp is a prime whose decimal digits, reversed, form a different prime. Both primality and the difference condition matter. This is a property of a number’s decimal representation, not a cipher by itself.

Examples and non-examples
13 and 31 form an emirp pair. 11 is prime but palindromic, so it is not an emirp under this definition. 23 is prime, but its reverse 32 is composite. The pair 7649 and 9467 passes both prime checks.
Keep decimal reversal distinct from mirroring an image, reversing rune order, complementing digits, and taking a prime ordinal. Decimal reversal of 8734 is 4378. A transformation from 8734 to 7649 therefore needs a separately specified rule; “invert” alone does not define it.

Where this matters in the manuscript
The spelling and prime-sum article computes the three LP2-57 body sentence totals under a declared rune-only convention and checks their reversals. The boundaries and counting convention belong to the claim. Finding an emirp after changing a boundary is a different test.

How to replicate the predicate
from math import isqrt
def prime(n):
    return n >= 2 and all(n % d for d in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1))
def emirp(n):
    reverse = int(str(n)[::-1]) if n >= 0 else -1
    return n != reverse and prime(n) and prime(reverse)
assert emirp(7649)
assert not emirp(11)
Converting the reversed digits to an integer removes leading zeros. This convention must be stated if applying reversal to strings that are not already prime numbers. See prime indices and selection effects.

Reproducing rune prime sums provides a read-only command and explicit spelling comparisons.
Sources and evidence
Exact sentence sums and conventions · Checked numerical examples. No authorial purpose follows from the emirp property alone.

---

Magic squares in the 2014 puzzle

Definitions, the historical 1033 square, and the later signed instructions.

A magic square has equal sums in every row, every column, and both main diagonals. Its order is its width and height; its magic constant is that common sum. Equal row sums alone are not enough.

Magic does not always mean normal
A normal order-n magic square uses each integer from 1 to n² exactly once. A general magic square need not use that range or distinct entries. Keep the definition separate from any additional rules in a historical challenge.

A documented 1033 square
The archived 2014 walkthrough records this order-5 square during an earlier puzzle stage:
272 138 341 131 151
366 199 130 320  18
226 245  91 245 226
 18 320 130 199 366
151 131 341 138 272
All five rows, all five columns, and both diagonals sum to 1033. Entries repeat, so it is not a normal square. This is historical context, not a newly discovered Liber Primus solution.

The later LP1 payloads
LP1-10 through LP1-13 contain signed instructions referring to three magic squares. Their ASCII borders differ. If one removes the surrounding border digits, the displayed interior is:
10 12 10
12 14 12
10 12 10
Its row sums are 32, 38, and 32. It is not itself a magic square under the definition above. Do not label the visible number arrangement as a solved magic square merely because the surrounding prose mentions them.
The historical walkthrough later describes an input form accepting squares subject to criteria, with an order-5 square summing to 3301 as one example. This wiki has not independently reconstructed the historical server validator. That report does not prove that the earlier 1033 square was the required submission.

The LP2-15 decimal panel is another distinct arrangement; its printed row and column sums are unequal.
How to check a square
n = len(square)
assert n and all(len(row) == n for row in square)
sums = [sum(row) for row in square]
sums += [sum(row[c] for row in square) for c in range(n)]
sums += [sum(square[i][i] for i in range(n)),
         sum(square[i][n-1-i] for i in range(n))]
is_magic = len(set(sums)) == 1
Run python scripts/check_number_examples.py to check all twelve lines of the historical 5 × 5 example. This checks arithmetic, not provenance or historical server acceptance.

Sources
Pinned 2014 walkthrough · LP1-10 body · All signed payloads and hashes.

https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/lp1-13.html

https://github.com/scream314/cicada3301/blob/10733feb487bb8beb9966d534727ee5897aa54fc/2014.md

The LP2-56 hash target

The exact printed value, its representation, and the assumptions a candidate check must state.

LP2-56 has a known reading titled “An End.” Its text refers to a page in the deep web that hashes to the hexadecimal value printed between the runic passages. Decoding the surrounding runes and finding the referenced page are separate tasks.

The literal target
The archived transcription preserves five printed rows:
36367763ab73783c7af284446c
59466b4cd653239a311cb7116
d4618dee09a8425893dc7500b
464fdaf1672d7bef5e891c6e227
4568926a49fb4f45132c2a8b4
Concatenating the rows yields 128 hexadecimal characters, representing 64 bytes, or 512 bits. The rows are presentation breaks; preserving them in a text file is different from the single digest string used for comparison.

Length is evidence of format, not proof of an algorithm
A SHA-512 digest has this length. The quoted decoded instruction does not name SHA-512 or define which bytes of a “page” should be hashed. Length alone cannot distinguish all algorithms that produce 512-bit outputs. State SHA-512 explicitly as an assumption when testing a candidate.
A URL string, an HTTP response body, an HTML source file, rendered text, and a screenshot are different inputs. Their hashes need not agree. Encoding, line endings, compression handling, and trailing newlines also matter. Do not silently normalize a candidate after a mismatch.

Extract the target from the shipped reading
import json, re
from pathlib import Path
page = json.loads(Path("data/pages/lp2-56.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
lines = [line.rstrip("/") for line in page["reading"]["literal"].splitlines()]
rows = [line for line in lines if re.fullmatch(r"[0-9a-f]+", line)]
target = "".join(rows)
assert len(rows) == 5 and len(target) == 128
assert len(bytes.fromhex(target)) == 64
print(target)
This extracts a preserved target. It does not discover a destination, query a network, or test candidate pages. Use the reading recipe to reproduce the surrounding text independently.

Record exactly what a candidate check establishes
A mismatch excludes the tested bytes under the chosen algorithm. It does not exclude every version of a site, every serialization, or every algorithm. A reported match should include the exact candidate bytes, their provenance, the hashing operation, and an independently repeatable comparison. See checksums and reproducibility.

Sources and status
Original image and reading · Structured record · Pinned walkthrough. The source snapshot establishes the known reading; this article does not assert that the referenced page has been located.

Sources, related references, and files
https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/lp2-56.html
https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/prime-minus-one.html
https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/checksums.html
https://jelliottdev.github.io/reference/articles/reproducibility.html
https://jelliottdev.github.io/#/reader/lp2-56
https://jelliottdev.github.io/data/pages/lp2-56.json

The LP2-15 number panel and heading

The exact 4 × 4 matrix, checked totals, red entry, heading, and open-loop drawing.

LP2-15 contains a red runic heading, a 4 × 4 decimal panel, and an open-loop drawing below it. Its combined archive index is 32. Use the release ID when citing it: LP1-15 is a different image with a known keyed reading.

The exact number panelValues in image order; row and column positions are one-based here.
	Row	Column 1	Column 2	Column 3	Column 4

	1	3258	3222	3152	3038

	2	3278	3299 (red)	3298	2838

	3	3288	3294	3296	2472

	4	4516	1206	708	1820

3299 is the only red number. 708 is the only three-digit entry. Preserve 4516 as printed; its being larger than 3301 is not a reason to change it. The structured page record stores the matrix in its numbers field.

Straightforward arithmetic
The row sums are 12670, 12713, 12350, and 8250. The column sums are 14340, 11021, 10454, and 10168. The two main diagonals sum to 11673 and 14146. All sixteen entries sum to 45983.
These unequal totals mean that the printed panel is not a magic square under the ordinary equal-line-sums definition. This says nothing about a proposed transformation of the entries; a transformed panel would be a different object and require its own stated rule.

The heading is not a known plaintext
The recorded heading has nine runes in groups of four and five: F U L M / A EA Y OE A. EA and OE each label a single rune. These are transliteration labels, not an English translation. The source snapshot does not establish “CRYING” or another plaintext for this heading.

The drawing below the panel
The page annotation describes two open lobes with a crossing, resembling an infinity sign; visible gaps remain. Shape resemblance does not establish that the author intended a particular Unicode character, its code point, or a numerical transformation of that code point. Keep the observed drawing separate from those proposed operations.

How to reproduce the totals
import json
from pathlib import Path
p = json.loads(Path("data/pages/lp2-15.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
a = p["numbers"]
assert len(a) == 4 and all(len(row) == 4 for row in a)
print("rows", [sum(row) for row in a])
print("columns", [sum(row[c] for row in a) for c in range(4)])
print("diagonals", sum(a[i][i] for i in range(4)),
      sum(a[i][3-i] for i in range(4)))
print("total", sum(map(sum, a)))
This is a check of the published transcription, not a cipher experiment or a new image audit. Compare the matrix to the original in the reader before using it as an input.

Following a numerical idea
The prime-index guide checks the arithmetic involving 3299, 30557, 9467, and 98597. The emirp guide distinguishes decimal reversal from mirroring and unspecified “inversion.” A valid calculation does not by itself connect LP2-15 with LP2-00–02. Record that proposed connection as a hypothesis with explicit operations and scope.

Sources
Original image, annotations, and archive provenance · Pinned number and rune transcription. Visual observations follow the existing page annotations; the totals above are derived arithmetic.

The two LP1 title pages

Visible Latin headings, the meaning of Intus, and the hidden-message chain.

The first release includes two title images among its seventeen pages. They are part of the file sequence and the hidden-message chain, even though neither has a runic paragraph.

LP1-00: Liber Primus
The cover displays “Liber Primus” in large black Latin lettering on a white field. The text sits above the vertical midpoint with broad margins. The literal visible text is recorded separately from the archived rune transcriptions; a rune count of zero does not mean the image contains no text or no information.

LP1-02: Chapter 1 — Intus
The chapter title displays “Chapter 1” above “Intus,” in black Latin lettering on white. The two text groups are vertically separated. In Latin, intus can mean “within” or “on the inside”; see the Lewis and Short dictionary entry. That lexical meaning does not by itself specify a cipher operation.

Both carry hidden messages
Each original JPEG yields a signed hexadecimal OutGuess body. Together with the warning image, LP1-01, they form the three-image XOR and transposition chain. Their visible headings and embedded bodies must remain separate in transcriptions and citations.

How to inspect the layers
Open the original image in the reader and compare its visible lettering with the labeled visible-text transcription.
Download the original JPEG, not the cropped thumbnail.
Follow OutGuess extraction and compare the expected checksum.
Verify the signed block, then follow the documented three-image chain.
The site’s title-page text is a labeled editorial transcription checked against the image on 19 October 2026. It is not a new cipher reading or a replacement for the image.

Sources
LP1-00 original and file provenance · LP1-02 original and file provenance · Hidden-payload evidence. Visual descriptions concern the displayed originals; no font identification or numerical interpretation of the layout is asserted.

The image hidden in LP1-03

The decoded JPEG, its archived rune transcription, and exact reproduction steps.

LP1-03 has two different images to examine: the visible runic manuscript page and a smaller JPEG encoded inside its signed OutGuess message. The known Vigenère reading of the manuscript does not automatically decode the second image.

The decoded derivativeThe JPEG decoded from the hexadecimal portion of LP1-03’s signed message.
The derivative is 587 × 109 pixels and 15,188 bytes. Download the JPEG. Its checksum is recorded in the payload manifest.

Archived transcription
The pinned iBotPeaches archive supplies this transcription:
ᚦᛗᛞᛇᚠᛗᚪᚱ5ᚢᚫᛝᚱᛝ3 ᛠᛗᛇᚠᛡ
It contains 18 runes and the decimal digits 5 and 3. In the wiki’s alphabet labels, with spaces inserted between individual symbols for clarity:
TH M D EO F M A R 5 U AE NG R NG 3 EA M EO F IA
Those labels are a transliteration, not established plaintext. The added spaces above identify symbol boundaries; they are not a new claim about word boundaries in the image. Decimal digits remain digits rather than becoming rune indices.

How to reproduce the image
First follow OutGuess extraction for LP1-03 and verify its signed message. Decode the hexadecimal suffix of the exported body:
from pathlib import Path
body = Path("exports/steganography/lp1-03.body.txt").read_text()
image = bytes.fromhex(body[body.index("ffd8ffe"):])
assert len(image) == 15188
with open("lp1-03-decoded.jpg", "xb") as output:
    output.write(image)
The exclusive-create mode refuses to overwrite an existing file. This reproduces a format conversion, not a proposed solution to the image’s text. Keep the original signed body and the derivative as separate files.

Sources
Pinned transcription of the embedded image · Signed block · Message body · Payload inventory.

LP2-00–02: text and image measurements

Rune regions, ink classes, punctuation shapes, and the limits of the stored visual survey.

LP2-00, LP2-01, and LP2-02 are the first three images of the second release. Their combined archive indices are 17–19. The source snapshot does not give them a known plaintext. Studying them together does not establish a shared key or a reset rule.

What has been measured
	Page	Rune regions	Red runes	Dark runes	Punctuation regions

	LP2-00	262	13	249	58

	LP2-01	266	0	266	62

	LP2-02	201	0	201	38

These are 729 stored rune regions and 158 punctuation regions. A region is a measurement unit, not necessarily a separate linguistic character. Rune counts refer to the archived transcription and its mapped image regions.

Punctuation has its own color and shape
LP2-00 has 56 one-component punctuation regions, one four-component region, and one thirteen-component region. One of its one-component marks and its thirteen-component mark are classified red. LP2-01 has 57 one-component and five four-component regions, all dark. LP2-02 has 36 one-component regions, one four-component region, and one thirteen-component region; the thirteen-component region is red.
Thus LP2-02 has no red rune regions but does have red punctuation. The recorded component count describes connected foreground pixels under a threshold, not the number of sentences, cipher shifts, or semantic separators. See image regions and connected components.

Layout details that affect inspection
LP2-00’s oversized opening S rune extends alongside the first three text rows. Its stored rectangle is [599, 664, 153, 501] in original-image pixels. Treating each horizontal row as independent can miss that shared visual context.
LP2-01’s recorded tenth visual row contains C/OE glyphs touching at their feet. Overlapping inspection rectangles preserve their context. A touching shape does not automatically merge the two transcription symbols.

Do not equate transcript punctuation with pixel shape
The archived ASCII notation can use the same period character for marks with different visual component counts. A period in exported text therefore does not prove that every corresponding mark has the same appearance. Keep transcription conventions, image observations, and a proposed reset rule separate.

How to inspect and reproduce the inventory
Open a page record and expand its recorded rune or punctuation regions.
Select “Inspect region” to view the recorded rectangle against the original image.
Use the page JSON’s visual.glyphs and visual.punctuation arrays to inspect the stored data.
Run the checks below from the repository root.
# Structural checks and stored counts; Python standard library:
python scripts/inspect_visual_records.py
# Fresh color/component recount within stored rectangles; requires Pillow:
python scripts/inspect_visual_records.py --pixels
If Pillow is not installed, install it with python -m pip install Pillow in your chosen Python environment. The pixel check verifies the original JPEG hashes before reading them. It does not generate new segmentation, decide which rune a shape represents, or test a cipher.

Evidence and limits
Measurement conventions and checked scope · Reproduction script · LP2-00 source record · LP2-01 source record · LP2-02 source record. Color classes and component counts were reproduced inside the published rectangles on 19 October 2026. This does not make the visual inventory exhaustive or establish a relationship with LP2-15’s number panel.
